cls: Antineoplastic - PD-1 blocking monoclonal antibody (immune checkpoint inhibitor)
pharm: Humanized IgG4 monoclonal antibody that binds the programmed death receptor-1 (PD-1) and blocks its interaction with ligands PD-L1 and PD-L2, releasing PD-1 pathway-mediated inhibition of the immune response and restoring T-cell antitumor activity.
quick: 200 mg IV every 3 weeks OR 400 mg IV every 6 weeks, infused over 30 minutes
Intravenous infusion; not related to meals
Can cause fetal harm (immune disruption); avoid in pregnancy
Do not breastfeed during treatment and for 4 months after the last dose
No dose adjustment for mild to moderate impairment; not studied in severe
No adjustment for mild impairment; not studied in moderate/severe; hold/discontinue for immune-mediated hepatitis
Immune-mediated reactions (lung, GI, liver, endocrine, renal, skin), thyroid/glucose, LFTs, creatinine, infusion reactions
summary: Pembrolizumab is a humanized IgG4 anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody (immune checkpoint inhibitor) used to treat a broad range of malignancies including melanoma, non-small cell lung cancer, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, classical Hodgkin lymphoma, urothelial carcinoma, MSI-H/dMMR and TMB-H tumors, renal cell carcinoma, triple-negative breast cancer, and others. The usual adult dose is 200 mg IV every 3 weeks or 400 mg IV every 6 weeks, each infused over 30 minutes. By blocking the PD-1 pathway it can cause immune-mediated adverse reactions affecting almost any organ - including pneumonitis, colitis, hepatitis, endocrinopathies (thyroid, adrenal insufficiency, hypophysitis, type 1 diabetes), nephritis, and dermatologic reactions - which may be severe or fatal and can occur at any time during or after treatment. It can also cause infusion-related reactions and serious complications of allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
indications: Unresectable or metastatic melanoma; adjuvant treatment of melanoma after complete resection
Non-small cell lung cancer (first-line and previously treated, alone or with chemotherapy per expression/biomarker status)
Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma and primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma
Microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) or mismatch repair deficient (dMMR) solid tumors and colorectal cancer
Gastric, esophageal, cervical, hepatocellular, renal cell, endometrial, and cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas (per labeled indications)
Triple-negative breast cancer (high-risk early-stage and locally recurrent/metastatic PD-L1-positive)

dosage.c: Adult solid tumors (single agent or combination)
dosage.d: 200 mg every 3 weeks OR 400 mg every 6 weeks
2 mg/kg (up to a maximum of 200 mg) every 3 weeks
Same pembrolizumab dose (200 mg q3w or 400 mg q6w); when given with chemotherapy, administer pembrolizumab first
Continue until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, or up to 24 months in patients without progression (or per indication-specific limits)
dosage.n: Adjuvant and curative-intent regimens have defined durations

admin: Administer as an intravenous infusion over 30 minutes through a sterile, non-pyrogenic, low-protein-binding 0.2 to 5 micron in-line or add-on filter
Dilute in 0.9% Sodium Chloride or 5% Dextrose to a final concentration of 1 to 10 mg/mL; do not shake
Do not co-administer other drugs through the same infusion line
When given with chemotherapy, infuse pembrolizumab first
Withhold, permanently discontinue, or treat with corticosteroids for immune-mediated reactions according to severity
Interrupt or slow the infusion rate for mild to moderate infusion reactions; stop and permanently discontinue for severe (Grade 3-4) reactions
moa: Pembrolizumab is a humanized monoclonal IgG4 kappa antibody that binds to the programmed death receptor-1 (PD-1) on T cells and blocks its interaction with the ligands PD-L1 and PD-L2. The PD-1 pathway is an immune checkpoint that normally limits T-cell activity in peripheral tissues; many tumors exploit it to evade immune detection. By blocking PD-1 binding, pembrolizumab releases this inhibition and reactivates tumor-specific T-cell-mediated immune responses, leading to antitumor activity. Because the same checkpoint normally restrains autoimmunity, this mechanism also underlies the broad spectrum of immune-mediated adverse reactions seen with therapy.

absolute: Known severe hypersensitivity to pembrolizumab or any excipient (per labeling, no other formal contraindications are listed)
relative: Active or history of immune-mediated disorders that may worsen with checkpoint blockade
Solid organ transplant recipients (risk of allograft rejection)
Patients who have undergone or will undergo allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (risk of severe transplant-related complications, including GVHD, hepatic veno-occlusive disease)
monitor: Immune-mediated reactions in any organ system (lung, colon, liver, endocrine glands, kidney, skin, and others)
Thyroid function, blood glucose, and adrenal/pituitary function
Infusion-related reactions during and after administration

preg: Based on its mechanism of action and animal data, pembrolizumab can cause fetal harm when administered to a pregnant woman; blocking the PD-1/PD-L1 pathway can disrupt maternal immune tolerance and increase the risk of immune-mediated rejection and fetal loss. Advise patients of the potential risk and use effective contraception during treatment and for 4 months after the last dose.
lact: There are no data on the presence of pembrolizumab in human milk or its effects on the breastfed infant. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions, advise patients not to breastfeed during treatment and for 4 months after the final dose.
renal: No dosage adjustment is recommended for patients with mild or moderate renal impairment. Pembrolizumab has not been studied in patients with severe renal impairment. Monitor renal function, as immune-mediated nephritis can occur.
hepatic: No dosage adjustment is recommended for patients with mild hepatic impairment. Pembrolizumab has not been studied in patients with moderate or severe hepatic impairment. Withhold or permanently discontinue for immune-mediated hepatitis based on severity, and monitor liver enzymes.

major: Systemic corticosteroids or other immunosuppressants before starting pembrolizumab may blunt efficacy - avoid baseline immunosuppression where possible (corticosteroids are used to treat immune-mediated reactions once they occur)
moderate: Live vaccines - avoid during immune checkpoint therapy due to uncertain safety/efficacy
Other immune checkpoint inhibitors or immunostimulatory agents - additive risk of immune-mediated toxicity
minor: No significant cytochrome P450-mediated small-molecule interactions established (monoclonal antibody)
interactions.alcohol: No direct interaction with alcohol established.
interactions.diagnostics: Obtain baseline and periodic thyroid function tests, blood glucose, liver enzymes, and serum creatinine; assess PD-L1 expression and/or MSI-H/dMMR/TMB-H status where required for the indication.

serious: Immune-mediated endocrinopathies - hypophysitis, thyroid disorders (hypo-/hyperthyroidism, thyroiditis), adrenal insufficiency, and type 1 diabetes mellitus including diabetic ketoacidosis
Immune-mediated dermatologic reactions including severe cutaneous reactions (SJS/TEN, DRESS)
Other immune-mediated reactions (myocarditis, pericarditis, neurologic - myasthenia/Guillain-Barre/encephalitis, ocular, pancreatitis, myositis, hematologic)
Complications of allogeneic HSCT (GVHD, hepatic veno-occlusive disease, severe and fatal transplant-related events)
rare: Severe immune-mediated myocarditis with fatal outcome
emergency: Colitis with severe diarrhea or bowel perforation
Myocarditis, severe infusion reaction/anaphylaxis, or SJS/TEN

monitoring: Evaluate for immune-mediated reactions in any organ system at baseline and periodically; investigate new or worsening symptoms promptly
Thyroid function tests, blood glucose, and adrenal/pituitary function
Liver enzymes and bilirubin before each cycle as indicated
Infusion-related reactions during and after administration; pulmonary symptoms for pneumonitis
counsel: This medicine works by activating your immune system, which can attack normal organs - report any new or worsening symptoms right away (cough, shortness of breath, diarrhea, abdominal pain, yellowing of skin/eyes, severe fatigue, excessive thirst/urination, rash, or muscle weakness)
Reactions can occur during treatment or even months after the last dose - keep all follow-up appointments and lab tests
Tell every provider you are receiving an immunotherapy so problems are managed correctly (often with steroids)
Tell your doctor if you have had an organ transplant or stem cell transplant, or an autoimmune disease
Use effective birth control during treatment and for 4 months after the last dose; do not breastfeed during this time
pk: Immune activation begins after first doses; tumor responses typically over weeks to months
Intravenous administration achieves peak serum concentration at end of the 30-minute infusion
Steady state reached by ~16 weeks with q3w dosing; effects can persist after discontinuation
Refrigerate at 2-8 C (36-46 F) in original carton to protect from light; do not freeze or shake; diluted solution per labeling
pearls: Immune-mediated adverse reactions can affect virtually any organ (pneumonitis, colitis, hepatitis, endocrinopathies, nephritis, dermatologic, cardiac, neurologic) and may be severe, fatal, and delayed - have a low threshold for evaluation and corticosteroids
Endocrinopathies (hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, hypophysitis, adrenal insufficiency, type 1 diabetes) are common - check TSH, glucose, and consider cortisol/ACTH at baseline and during therapy
Manage most immune-mediated reactions by withholding or discontinuing the drug and starting corticosteroids, tapering once improved
Severe or fatal allogeneic HSCT complications (GVHD, veno-occlusive disease) can occur in patients with prior or subsequent transplant
Two equivalent adult schedules: 200 mg IV every 3 weeks or 400 mg IV every 6 weeks - confirm the schedule and dilution before each infusion
missed: There is no patient self-administered dose. If a scheduled infusion is missed or delayed, the treating oncology team reschedules it as soon as feasible and resumes the every-3-week or every-6-week interval; contact the oncology clinic for rescheduling rather than skipping evaluation.
overdose: There is no information on overdose with pembrolizumab. In the event of overdose, monitor the patient closely for signs or symptoms of adverse reactions, particularly immune-mediated reactions, and institute appropriate symptomatic treatment, including corticosteroids as indicated.
